Hi Sofia,

Thanks again for taking this — we want to size reserved capacity for a planned production rollout of our enterprise contextual search product. High-level items:
- Model: internally validated LLaMA-variant ~70B (we may accept a Redwood-verified 70B open model variant).
- Typical request profile: 40 QPS peak (short bursts to 120 QPS), expected average seq: 1.2k tokens, but we must support retrieval-augmented queries that expand to 50–70k context tokens (tokenized) for long documents.
- SLA target: 95% of requests < 200ms p50 and < 500ms p99 for generation path (we understand long-context ops may be higher).
- Accuracy tolerance: willing to accept small delta if we can get 2–3x cost reduction via quantization.
- Procurement: looking at a 12‑month reserved capacity contract; need an initial sizing for the SOW + pricing.

Attached is our workbook with sample trace data (Aurora_capacity_workbook_v2.xlsx). Key asks: 1) recommended reserved GPU types/count for baseline + canary, 2) guidance on how quantization and KV cache strategy change GPU counts and failure modes, 3) rough committed spend estimate.

Can you loop in your infra folks? Happy to jump on a technical deep-dive Thurs.

Best,

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
To: Sofia Ivanova <sofia_ivanova@redwood.ai>, Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Dedicated sizing ask — Aurora contextual search (70k context)

Folks — ran a quick sim based on Claire's workbook (thanks) + internal profiling of a 70B family model. High-level TL;DR then detail below:

TL;DR
- If Aurora requires full 70k in-GPU KV for all requests, expect per-replica GPU footprint: model weights + KV ≈ 1x A100-80GB (weights via 4-bit quant) + KV sharded across 3–4 GPUs for latency target -> effectively 4 GPUs per replica. That gives ~200–300ms median on our bench for generation with batched QPS ~20/replica.
- Cost-optimized path (aggressive 4-bit quant, NVMe KV offload, routing long-tail to multi-GPU batch worker) reduces dedicated GPUs to ~1–2 GPUs per replica but increases p99 and adds host/NVMe IO variability.
- Recommended start: Canary: 3 replicas x 4 GPUs (12 GPUs) on A100-80GB; Production commit: 4 replicas x 12 GPUs (48 GPUs) to handle 40 QPS baseline with burst headroom and rolling upgrades.

Assumptions and numbers
- Model weights memory (70B family):
  - FP16 baseline: ~140 GB (not viable on single GPU).
  - 8-bit weight compression: ~70 GB.
  - 4-bit weight compression (quant-aware runtime): ~35–40 GB. We assume an efficient 4-bit kernel so model weights fit across 1–2 80GB devices (model sharded + offload).

- KV cache sizing: KV scales roughly linearly with token count. For this model profile we measured ~0.95 GB per 1k tokens (this includes keys+values + per-layer overhead).
  - 5k tokens -> ~4.8 GB; 50k tokens -> ~47.5 GB; 70k tokens -> ~66.5 GB.
  - For in-GPU KV (no offload), that implies 70k requests need ~66 GB extra on top of weights per request shard — so we shard KV across GPUs or reserve multiple GPUs per in-flight request.

- Memory layout/options:
  1) In-GPU KV sharding: split KV across 3–4 GPUs, each holding ~16–25 GB KV chunk + part of weights. Best for latency but requires more GPUs and careful TP/PP placement.
  2) NVMe/host offload: keep model weights on GPU (4-bit) and stream KV from NVMe into GPU when needed. Reduces GPU count but adds ~50–150ms variance depending on IO and concurrency; also increases NVMe throughput requirements.
  3) Prefix/cache prewarming: for many support workloads we can keep hot prefixes in GPU and only offload cold contexts. This hybrid reduces average KV footprint but requires workload predictability.

- Quantization tradeoffs:
  - Moving to 4-bit (vs 8-bit) reduces weights memory ~2x and enables single-GPU weight residency in many cases, but requires specialized kernels and can increase generation latency per-token slightly (~3–8ms per token).
  - We measured < $0.5% top-line quality drop on our evals for Aurora-like RAG tasks, but we should run a short A/B with Aurora eval prompts.

Fleet sizing example (peak 40 QPS):
- Latency-optimized (option B):
  - Replica footprint: 4 x A100-80GB GPUs (in-GPU KV sharded), 1 replica handles ~18–25 QPS depending on batching.
  - To hit 40 QPS with headroom, 3 replicas (12 GPUs). Add rolling upgrade buffer => 4 replicas => 16 GPUs. Our safe production commit recommendation (to absorb bursts and scheduled maintenance) is 48 GPUs (4 groups of 12) for the contract size you described.

- Cost-optimized (option A):
  - Replica footprint: 1–2 x A100-80GB GPUs (4-bit weights), KV offloaded to NVMe nodes. Each replica handles higher batched throughput but has increased tail latency and variability. For the same QPS consider 12–16 GPUs across fewer replicas but with higher NVMe capacity.

Operational & failure modes
- If a GPU node with in-GPU KV fails, requests touching that shard will see increased fallback latency or need re-routing to the slow path — design automatic fallback to NVMe-backed replicas.
- Quantization-specific: rolling upgrades between quant modes must run evals; hot swap between 8-bit/4-bit variants can be used as a safety net.

I'll prepare a short one-pager comparing the two options and a back-of-envelope committed monthly cost by EOD.

- Marcus

Claire — answers inline:
1) p99 estimates (50k–70k token request):
   - In-GPU KV sharded across 3–4 x A100-80GB: p99 generation ~= 400–700ms depending on batch size (small batches lower p50 but p99 dominated by KV fetch + attention compute).
   - NVMe offload approach: p99 generation ~= 800–1500ms for cold reads; with aggressive prefetch + NVMe tiering we can bring cold p99 down to ~700–900ms. Warm/prefetched keys reduce both approaches significantly.

2) 48 GPU breakdown (assumes 4-bit quant for weights unless otherwise noted):
   - Primary region (us-west-2): 36 x A100-80GB (3 availability zones, spread across AZs for redundancy).
   - Failover region (us-east-1): 12 x A100-80GB as warm standby (can be partially on 8-bit variants for cost).
   - This gives you 3 AZs with capacity to run replicas + rolling upgrade headroom.

I'll put together a short slide with these numbers + recommended NVMe sizing and SLO impact to share in the deep-dive. Marcus + Mina plan to join Thursday 10am PT.

-Marcus
